title: Case study: the Ohorongo cement works

blocks.heading: The case study: a real factory
blocks.text: A required case study of one real factory at the scale the syllabus asks for: the Ohorongo cement works near Otavi in northern Namibia - what it is, why it is located there, and how it works as an industrial system.

blocks.heading: The works and its place
blocks.text: The Ohorongo cement works stands beside Otavi, a small town on Namibia's north-south railway in the Otjozondjupa region. Production began in 2011 after an investment of about N$2.5 billion, one of the largest private industrial projects in the country's history, and the works employs around 300 permanent workers (2010s figure), with many more during the building phase. Its raw material is local: marble-rich rock is cut at a quarry beside the works and fed to the kilns. The works is thus a factory with its inputs at hand - the quarry on site, the workforce in the town next door, and the railway a short haul away.

blocks.heading: Why Otavi?
blocks.text: Each location factor earns its place. Raw material: the quarry sits beside the works, and cement-making is bulk-losing - well over a tonne of rock goes into each tonne of cement - so the works belongs at the rock face, not hauling stone for hundreds of kilometres. Transport: Otavi is a railway junction, so fuel and equipment arrive by rail and cement leaves the same way, north to the towns of the region and south towards the coast. Labour and services: the town supplies workers, water and power connections without new building. Market: northern Namibia's growing towns and building trade lie close by, and cement is costly to carry far, so a works near its buyers keeps delivery journeys short.

blocks.heading: The works as a system
blocks.text: The same factory drawn as an industrial system: inputs of quarry rock, kiln fuel, electricity, water and labour from Otavi; processes that crush and grind the rock, burn it into clinker in the kilns, then grind it again with additives into cement; outputs of bagged and bulk cement for the building trade, plus the waste streams, kiln gases, dust caught by filters, and warm air. The three-part pattern from the first section, now filled with a real place.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The kilns burn fuel, which ties the works to the energy sources of topic 3.5, and the dust and gases raise the environmental risks of topic 3.7. Its jobs are part of the employment structure of topic 3.1.
